domain:
    # Matrix dimensions (following PolyBench naming)
    i: dim in [0, M)      # row index,  0 <= i < m
    j: dim in [0, N)      # column index, 0 <= j < n
    k: dim in [0, N)      # current Gram–Schmidt column, 0 <= k < n

data:
    # All matrices are stored row-major in C: A[i][j] ~ A[i * N + j]
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # Input:  original m×n matrix.
        # Output: overwritten in-place by the evolving residuals A^(k),
        #         as in the PolyBench reference/MGS algorithm.
    R[k, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j
        # Upper-triangular n×n matrix; only entries with k <= j are used.
    Q[i, k]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * N + k
        # Orthonormal m×n matrix; columns form an orthonormal basis.
    # Scalar temporaries, reused for each k
    nrm: DATA_TYPE
    invR: DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    # Tunable blocking and SIMD parameters for the inner work.
    Ti_nrm: int    # tile size over rows in the column-norm reduction
    Ti:     int    # tile size over rows in projection/update phases
    Tj:     int    # tile size over trailing columns j > k
    V:      int    # SIMD width used when vectorizing across j

computation:
    # Classical modified Gram–Schmidt (MGS) with improved loop structure.
    #
    # For each column k:
    #   1. Compute its 2-norm based on the current residual A[:, k].
    #   2. Normalize to obtain Q[:, k] and R[k, k].
    #   3. For each later column j > k:
    #        - Compute R[k, j] = Q[:, k]^T A[:, j]
    #        - Update A[:, j] <- A[:, j] - Q[:, k] * R[k, j]
    #
    # This matches the Exo kernel’s semantics exactly (up to FP
    # rounding), but with a schedule that favors row-major access.

    for k in seq(0, N):

        # 1. Column norm:
        #    nrm = sum_{i=0}^{M-1} A[i, k]^2
        nrm = sum(i, A[i, k] * A[i, k])

        # 2. Normalize to get Q[:, k] and R[k, k].
        R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm)

        # Precompute reciprocal once: replace M divisions by one division + M multiplies.
        # Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k]  ≈  A[i, k] * (1 / R[k, k])
        invR = 1.0 / R[k, k]

        for i in seq(0, M):
            Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * invR
            # After this, A[:, k] is never read again in the algorithm;
            # it can be left as-is or overwritten by Q[:, k] without
            # changing later computations.

        # 3. Orthogonalize the remaining columns j > k against Q[:, k].

        # 3.0 Initialize the row k of R above the diagonal.
        for j in seq(k + 1, N):
            R[k, j] = 0.0

        # 3.1 Dot products (projection coefficients)
        #     R[k, j] = sum_i Q[i, k] * A[i, j]
        #
        #     Scheduled with i outer and j inner so that:
        #       - A[i, j] and R[k, j] are accessed with unit stride in j,
        #         matching row-major layout.
        #       - Q[i, k] is loaded once per row i and reused over all j.
        for i in seq(0, M):
            qik = Q[i, k]                 # kept in a register
            for j in seq(k + 1, N):
                R[k, j] += qik * A[i, j]

        # 3.2 Rank-1 update
        #     A[:, j] <- A[:, j] - Q[:, k] * R[k, j]
        #
        #     Same row-major-friendly (i, j) ordering for good locality:
        #       - A[i, j] updated with unit-stride writes in the innermost loop.
        #       - R[k, j] reused from cache across all rows.
        for i in seq(0, M):
            qik = Q[i, k]
            for j in seq(k + 1, N):
                A[i, j] -= qik * R[k, j]

optimization:
    # Goal: exploit row-major layout, caches, SIMD, and multicore parallelism
    # without changing the Gram–Schmidt numerical behavior.

    # 1. Column-norm reduction (nrm):
    #
    #    nrm = sum(i, A[i, k] * A[i, k])
    #
    #    - Tile over i so each thread works on contiguous row-chunks of A[:, k].
    #    - Parallelize across tiles with a reduction on nrm.
    #    - Vectorize the inner loop over i to use SIMD loads of A[i, k].
    block(i, I_nrm, Ti_nrm)        # for the nrm computation: i = I_nrm * Ti_nrm + ii
    parallelize(I_nrm)             # parallel tiles; reduction on nrm
    vectorize(i, V)                # SIMD over rows in each tile

    # 2. Projection (3.1) and update (3.2) phases:
    #
    #    Both phases already use an (i outer, j inner) order that:
    #      - Streams across each row A[i, k+1: N) with unit-stride access.
    #      - Reuses qik = Q[i, k] across all j for that row.
    #      - Accesses R[k, j] with unit-stride in j (row k of R).
    #
    #    We further:
    #      - Tile rows (i) and trailing columns (j > k) to improve cache reuse.
    #      - Hoist tile loops so that each tile is processed as a block per k.
    #      - Parallelize across row tiles; in the projection phase this is a
    #        reduction on R[k, j] over I-tiles, while the update phase is
    #        embarrassingly parallel across I-tiles.
    #      - Vectorize j inside each tile to map cleanly to SIMD.
    block(i, I, Ti)                # tile rows in 3.1 and 3.2
    block(j, J, Tj)                # tile trailing columns (j in [k+1, N))
    hoist(I)                       # make row-tile loop outermost within each k
    hoist(J)                       # next-outer: column-tile loop

    parallelize(I)                 # parallel over row tiles:
                                   #  - dot phase: reduction on R[k, j] across I
                                   #  - update phase: independent updates across I
    vectorize(j, V)                # SIMD within each tile across contiguous columns

    # 3. Scalar-strength reduction:
    #
    #    - Keep invR = 1 / R[k, k] and qik = Q[i, k] in registers within their
    #      respective scopes.
    #    - This replaces M divisions by one division + M multiplies per k, and
    #      avoids redundant loads of Q[i, k] inside the inner j-loops, while
    #      preserving the mathematical Gram–Schmidt computation.

```text
domain:
    # Matrix dimensions: m rows, n columns, with m >= n in the typical PolyBench setup.
    i: dim in [0, M)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # A: input matrix, overwritten in-place during Gram–Schmidt.
    # Row-major layout matches the PolyBench C arrays.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # R: upper-triangular factor. Only R[k, j] for 0 <= k <= j < N are non-zero on exit.
    # Row-major layout; rows R[k, :] are contiguous, which is useful since we always access
    # entries along a fixed row k.
    R[k, j]: out DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j

    # Q: orthonormal columns. We store Q in column-major form to make each column Q[:, k]
    # contiguous in memory, exploiting spatial locality for column-wise operations.
    Q[i, j]: out DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i

    # Local scalars used inside the per-k iteration.
    nrm:    local DATA_TYPE   # squared 2-norm of column k of A
    inv_rk: local DATA_TYPE   # 1 / R[k, k], to turn divides into multiplies

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (match m and n in the C driver).
    M: size
    N: size

    # Tunable performance parameters (chosen to fit the cache/SIMD widths of the target).
    TILE_J:   size  # tile size along the trailing-column dimension j (e.g., 32–128)
    VEC_J:    size  # SIMD width along j (e.g., 4/8/16, depending on DATA_TYPE and ISA)
    UNROLL_I: size  # unroll factor for loops over i (e.g., 4 or 8)

computation:
    # Classical Gram–Schmidt (without reorthogonalization).
    # Outer loop over k must remain sequential: each new column uses the updated A and
    # previously computed Q[:, 0..k-1].
    for k in seq(0, N):

        # 1. Compute the 2-norm of the k-th column of A:
        #        nrm = sum_{i=0}^{M-1} A[i, k]^2
        nrm = sum(i, A[i, k] * A[i, k])

        # 2. Normalize column k: R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm), Q[:, k] = A[:, k] / R[k, k].
        R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm)

        # Instead of dividing every element of A[:, k] by R[k, k], compute its reciprocal
        # once and use multiplications:
        inv_rk = 1.0 / R[k, k]

        for i in seq(0, M):
            Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * inv_rk

        # 3. For each trailing column j > k, project onto Q[:, k] and deflate A[:, j]:
        #
        #    R[k, j] = Q[:, k]^T * A[:, j] = sum_i Q[i, k] * A[i, j]
        #    A[:, j] = A[:, j] - Q[:, k] * R[k, j]
        #
        # The following is the direct, sequential specification. The optimization section
        # will describe a cache- and SIMD-friendly schedule for these operations.
        for j in seq(k + 1, N):
            # Projection coefficient (dot product).
            R[k, j] = sum(i, Q[i, k] * A[i, j])

            # Rank-1 update of column j.
            for i in seq(0, M):
                A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

optimization:
    # Storage/layout optimizations
    # ----------------------------
    # Q is stored column-major (see data section), so each Q[:, k] is contiguous:
    #   Q[i, k] -> base_Q + k * M + i
    # This aligns the normalization and projection steps, which are column-based,
    # with unit-stride memory accesses for Q.

    # Arithmetic optimization
    # -----------------------
    # The computation already reflects a key micro-optimization:
    #   - Replace M per-element divisions Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k]
    #     with one division inv_rk = 1 / R[k, k] and M multiplications
    #     Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * inv_rk.
    # This reduces the number of expensive divide operations while preserving
    # mathematical semantics.

    # Tiling and loop reordering for the trailing update (j > k)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # For each fixed k, the work over trailing columns j in [k+1, N) is independent
    # across j: R[k, j] and A[:, j] for different j do not interfere. We exploit this
    # by tiling and reordering loops over j so that:
    #   - We get cache-friendly, unit-stride access to A and R along the j dimension.
    #   - We expose coarse-grain parallelism across independent column tiles.
    #
    # The following directives conceptually apply to the two uses of "for j in seq(k+1, N)"
    # in the computation (the projection and the rank-1 update), within each fixed k.

    # 1. Tile the trailing-column dimension j into tiles of size TILE_J.
    block(j, J, TILE_J)
    # After blocking, each "trailing-column" loop is over tiles J and inner indices j_in_J.

    # 2. Hoist the tile loop J to be outermost inside each fixed k, so that we work on
    # one band of columns at a time. This improves temporal locality for A and R.
    hoist(J)

    # 3. Within each (k, J) tile, reorder the i and j loops so that j is the innermost
    # dimension when traversing row-major arrays A and R:
    #
    #     for i in ...
    #         for j in ...
    #             ... A[i, j] ..., R[k, j] ...
    #
    # This yields unit-stride access in memory along j for A[i, j] and R[k, j], which
    # is ideal for cache lines and vector loads. (Floating-point reductions over i are
    # reassociated accordingly.)
    interchange(j, i)

    # 4. Vectorize the innermost loops over j inside each (k, J) tile. Because j now
    # corresponds to contiguous memory locations in both A and R, SIMD loads and stores
    # are efficient.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)

    # 5. Unroll the remaining loops over i by a small factor to increase ILP and reduce
    # loop overhead while keeping register pressure reasonable.
    unroll(i, UNROLL_I)

    # Parallelization
    # ---------------
    # For each fixed k, tiles J of the trailing columns are independent:
    #   - Each tile owns a disjoint subset of columns j.
    #   - For each j, the projection R[k, j] is a reduction over i that touches only that
    #     column of A and that entry of R.
    #   - The subsequent rank-1 update modifies only A[:, j] in that same tile and reads
    #     only R[k, j] and Q[:, k].
    #
    # Therefore, we can safely parallelize across J tiles for a fixed k, without
    # introducing cross-thread dependencies. Each thread computes the reductions for
    # R[k, j] in its own tile and then updates the corresponding columns of A.
    parallelize(J)

    # The outer loop over k remains sequential, preserving the dependence structure
    # of the Gram–Schmidt process: column k+1 must see the A matrix that has already
    # been deflated by columns 0..k.
```

domain:
    # Matrix dimensions: m rows, n columns, with 0 <= n <= m in usual QR usage.
    i: dim in [0, M)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index
    k: dim in [0, N)          # Gram–Schmidt step (current column)

data:
    # All matrices are stored in standard C row-major order:
    #   row i, col j  ↦  i * N + j
    #
    # A is modified in-place to hold the progressively orthogonalized
    # “residual” columns; its final value is part of the live-out state.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # R is upper triangular; entries R[p, q] with p > q remain zero.
    R[i, j]: out DATA_TYPE    = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Q holds the orthonormal basis vectors as columns Q[:, k].
    Q[i, j]: out DATA_TYPE    = (i, j) -> i * N + j

parameters:
    M: int  # number of rows
    N: int  # number of columns
    # Tunable blocking / vectorization parameters (chosen for target machine).
    T_M: int  # tile size in the row dimension i, 1 <= T_M <= M
    T_N: int  # tile size in the trailing-column dimension j, 1 <= T_N <= N
    V:   int  # preferred SIMD width for inner j loops (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float)

    # External scalar operation:
    #   sqrt(x): DATA_TYPE -> DATA_TYPE
    # implemented by a math library call, e.g., libm sqrtf/sqrt.
    # It is side-effect free.

computation:
    # Classical Gram–Schmidt QR factorization of A (M×N) into Q (M×N) and R (N×N).
    # This version is already written in an optimized loop order that respects
    # row‑major storage: when possible, inner loops traverse j (columns) so that
    # A[i, j] and R[k, j] are accessed with unit stride.

    # Precondition / initialization (conceptual; in the driver this is done
    # in init_array):
    #   for all i, j: R[i, j] = 0
    # Q may be left uninitialized before the kernel.

    for k in seq(0, N):                    # process column k

        # 1) Compute squared 2‑norm of column A[:, k].
        #    nrm_k = sum_{i=0}^{M-1} A[i, k]^2
        nrm_k: scalar DATA_TYPE
        nrm_k = 0
        for i in seq(0, M):
            nrm_k += A[i, k] * A[i, k]

        # 2) Set diagonal of R and normalize column k to form Q[:, k].
        R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm_k)

        # 3) Initialize the rest of row k of R (strict upper triangle) to zero.
        #    Only indices j > k will be written and later used.
        for j in seq(k + 1, N):
            R[k, j] = 0

        # 4) Fuse normalization of column k with accumulation of row k of R.
        #
        #    After this loop:
        #      Q[i, k]   = A[i, k] / R[k, k]
        #      R[k, j]  += Q[:, k]^T * A[:, j]  for all j > k
        #
        #    Loop order is i outer, j inner:
        #      - A[i, k] is accessed with stride N (column access) — unavoidable.
        #      - A[i, j] and R[k, j] are accessed with unit stride along j,
        #        matching row‑major layout and enabling cache‑friendly streaming.
        for i in seq(0, M):
            aik = A[i, k]
            qik = aik / R[k, k]
            Q[i, k] = qik
            for j in seq(k + 1, N):
                R[k, j] += qik * A[i, j]

        # 5) Update the trailing columns A[:, j] for j > k:
        #      A[:, j] ← A[:, j] − Q[:, k] * R[k, j]
        #
        #    We choose row‑major traversal: i outer, j inner.
        #    This preserves the mathematical result of the original Exo kernel
        #    (up to floating-point re-association) because each (k, j) update
        #    depends only on Q[:, k] and A[:, j] as they were at the start of
        #    step k, and columns j > k are independent of each other during step k.
        for i in seq(0, M):
            qik = Q[i, k]                   # reuse normalized value
            for j in seq(k + 1, N):
                A[i, j] -= qik * R[k, j]


optimization:
    # High-level goal:
    #   - Preserve the triangular, column‑by‑column dependency structure in k.
    #   - Within each fixed k, exploit the fact that:
    #       * Reductions over i (nrm_k and R[k, j]) are associative.
    #       * Updates of different columns j > k are independent.
    #   - Restructure loops so the heavy work uses row‑major, stride‑1 memory
    #     access and exposes vectorization and parallelism on i and j.

    # 1. Loop restructuring for locality (already reflected in 'computation').
    #
    #    a) For the dot products R[k, j] = Q[:, k]^T A[:, j], start from the
    #       naive column‑centric version:
    #           for j in (k+1 .. N):
    #               R[k, j] = sum_i Q[i, k] * A[i, j]
    #       and apply loop interchange:
    #           interchange(i, j_R_accum)
    #       to obtain:
    #           for i in [0, M):
    #               for j in (k+1 .. N):
    #                   R[k, j] += Q[i, k] * A[i, j]
    #       giving row‑major access to A and R.
    #
    #    b) For the A update, start from the original:
    #           for j in (k+1 .. N):
    #               for i in [0, M):
    #                   A[i, j] -= Q[i, k] * R[k, j]
    #       and apply:
    #           interchange(i, j_A_update)
    #       yielding:
    #           for i in [0, M):
    #               for j in (k+1 .. N):
    #                   A[i, j] -= Q[i, k] * R[k, j]
    #       again enabling stride‑1 access to A and R along j.
    #
    #    c) Fuse the loop that normalizes column k of Q with the loop that
    #       accumulates R[k, j], as in the 'computation' section, to avoid
    #       re-reading Q[:, k] for the dot products and to keep qik in a
    #       register across the inner j-loop.

    # 2. Blocking (tiling) to improve cache reuse.
    #
    #    Tile the row dimension i in all loops that traverse rows, using a
    #    tunable tile size T_M. This improves reuse of a row of A and Q across
    #    multiple columns j and exposes a coarse-grain unit for parallelism.
    #
    block(i, I, T_M)
    hoist(I)  # hoist the tile loop I to be outermost within each fixed k

    #    Tile the trailing columns j > k into column blocks of size T_N so that
    #    each block A[*, J:J+T_N) and the corresponding R[k, J:J+T_N) fit
    #    comfortably into cache during both accumulation and update phases.
    #
    #    Conceptually, within each k:
    #        for J in blocks of (k+1 .. N) by T_N:
    #            # R accumulation over this tile
    #            for i in ...
    #                for j in J .. min(J+T_N, N):
    #                    ...
    #            # A update over this tile
    #            for i in ...
    #                for j in J .. min(J+T_N, N):
    #                    ...
    #
    block(j, J, T_N)

    # 3. Parallelism.
    #
    #    The outer k-loop is inherently sequential:
    #      - Step k depends on the updated A produced by all previous steps p < k.
    #    However, within a fixed k, we have:
    #      - nrm_k as a reduction over i,
    #      - R[k, j] as a reduction over i for each j,
    #      - A updates independent across i for a given j and across j for a given i.
    #
    #    We thus parallelize over the row-tiles I for:
    #      - the norm computation,
    #      - the fused normalization/R-accumulation loop,
    #      - the trailing A update,
    #    using reduction semantics for nrm_k and R[k, j].
    #
    #    Implementation-wise this is a parallel-for over I with private partial
    #    accumulators:
    #        nrm_k_thread, R_thread[k, J:J+T_N)
    #    followed by a tree reduction into the shared nrm_k and R[k, J:J+T_N).
    #
    parallelize(I)

    # 4. Vectorization.
    #
    #    Inner loops over the column index j traverse contiguous memory in both
    #    A[i, j] and R[k, j], making them ideal SIMD candidates. We rely on the
    #    compiler’s autovectorizer but also express the intent explicitly:
    #
    #      - Vectorize inner j-loops in both the R accumulation and A update.
    #      - Use vector width V appropriate to the target ISA (e.g., V = 8
    #        for AVX2 single precision, V = 4 for AVX2 double precision).
    #
    vectorize(j, V)

    # 5. Scalar and register optimizations.
    #
    #    - Keep qik = Q[i, k] or (A[i, k] / R[k, k]) in a scalar register
    #      across the inner j loops to avoid redundant loads of Q[i, k].
    #    - Similarly, keep R[k, j] values in registers inside the innermost
    #      j-vector loops when updating A[i, j].
    #
    #    These are realized automatically when fusing the loops as in the
    #    'computation' section and after tiling; no extra storage is required.

    # 6. Memory footprint.
    #
    #    - No additional large temporary matrices are introduced; all work is
    #      done in-place on A, R, and Q.
    #    - Temporary storage is limited to per-tile / per-thread scalars or
    #      short vectors for partial reductions (nrm_k and small slices of
    #      R[k, j]), whose total size is negligible compared to A, R, and Q.
    #
    #    Therefore, the total memory footprint remains within well under 50%
    #    overhead relative to the original A (M×N), R (N×N), and Q (M×N).

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # A is updated in-place during orthogonalization.
    # Store A and Q in column-major to make inner loops over i unit-stride.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i      # column-major
    Q[i, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> j * M + i      # column-major

    # R is small (N×N) and mostly accessed by rows (fixed k, varying j),
    # so we keep it row-major.
    R[i, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j      # row-major

parameters:
    # Problem sizes
    M: size
    N: size

    # Tuning constants (chosen to respect cache/SIMD characteristics)
    T_I: size      # tile size for row dimension i, fits into L1/L2
    T_J: size      # tile size for column dimension j in the trailing panel
    VEC_LEN: size  # SIMD width for vectorization along i (e.g., 4 or 8)
    UNROLL_I: size # small unroll factor for innermost i loops

computation:
    # Classical Gram–Schmidt with in-place updates to A.
    for k in seq(0, N):
        # 1) Compute the 2-norm of column k of A.
        R[k, k] = sqrt(
            sum(i in [0, M): A[i, k] * A[i, k])
        )

        # 2) Normalize column k into Q.
        for i in [0, M):
            Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k]

        # 3) For each j > k, project A[:, j] onto Q[:, k] and subtract.
        for j in [k + 1, N):
            # R[k, j] = Q[:, k]^T * A[:, j]
            R[k, j] = sum(i in [0, M): Q[i, k] * A[i, j])

            # A[:, j] = A[:, j] - Q[:, k] * R[k, j]
            for i in [0, M):
                A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

optimization:
    # 1) Improve cache locality and enable reuse via blocking.
    #
    # Block the row dimension i wherever it appears (norms, dot products,
    # and updates), so that each tile of A(:, j) and Q(:, k) works on
    # a chunk that fits into L1/L2 cache.
    block(i, I, T_I)
    # Block the trailing-column dimension j in the k-phase. This lets us
    # operate on a panel of columns at once while keeping R[k, j] and the
    # corresponding A(:, j) columns hot in cache.
    block(j, J, T_J)

    # Hoist the outer tile loops so we iterate over tiles before elements.
    # This yields a structure roughly like:
    #   for k:
    #     for J:
    #       for I:
    #         inner i-loop over the tile
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # 2) Exploit parallelism.
    #
    # For each fixed k, different columns j > k are independent:
    #   - R[k, j] uses only Q[:, k] and A[:, j]
    #   - The update of A[:, j] uses only Q[:, k] and R[k, j]
    # Hence we can parallelize over tiled J (or j) when computing
    # the projections and updates.
    parallelize(J)
    # Within each tile, loops over i are either:
    #   - pure element-wise updates (Q[i, k], A[i, j]), or
    #   - part of a sum() reduction (for R[k, k] and R[k, j]).
    # We parallelize the I / i dimension with appropriate reduction
    # handling where sum() appears.
    parallelize(I)

    # 3) SIMD vectorization and unrolling along the inner-most i.
    #
    # With column-major A and Q, inner loops over i are unit-stride and
    # ideal for SIMD. Vectorize those loops, and lightly unroll to
    # increase ILP for the FMA-based dot products and updates.
    vectorize(i, VEC_LEN)
    unroll(i, UNROLL_I)
```

Here is an optimized model description for the Exo Gram–Schmidt kernel:

```text
domain:
    # m: number of rows (vectors live in ℝ^m)
    # n: number of columns (number of vectors)
    i: dim in [0, M)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # All 2D arrays are stored in row-major layout, as in the C/PolyBench driver.
    # A is updated in place during the algorithm (trailing columns get orthogonalized).
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j      # M×N, row-major
    Q[i, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j      # M×N, row-major
    R[k, j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j      # N×N, row-major, upper-triangular at the end

parameters:
    # Problem sizes.
    M: size
    N: size

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters.
    TI: size    # block size in the row dimension (i), e.g., 128 or 256
    TJ: size    # block size in the column dimension (j), e.g., 32 or 64
    VJ: size    # SIMD vector width in the j dimension (columns), e.g., 8 for AVX2 float
    T:  size    # maximum number of parallel threads for column tiles

computation:
    # Modified Gram–Schmidt: A ≈ Q R, with Q having orthonormal columns and R upper triangular.
    # We keep the mathematically exact order of inner products per (k, j): the sum over i
    # is still accumulated in increasing i, so FP rounding behavior per dot-product matches
    # the reference algorithm.

    for k in [0, N):
        # 1. Compute R[k, k] = ||A[:, k]||_2.
        #    This is the Euclidean norm of column k of the *current* A.
        #
        #    nrm_k = Σ_{i=0}^{M-1} A[i, k]^2
        #    R[k, k] = sqrt(nrm_k)
        R[k, k] = sqrt( sum(i in [0, M), A[i, k] * A[i, k]) )

        # 2. Normalize the k-th column: Q[:, k] = A[:, k] / R[k, k].
        #    (A is not modified here; it is used as the source vector.)
        for i in [0, M):
            Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k]

        # 3. Orthogonalize trailing columns j > k against q_k = Q[:, k].
        #
        #    For each j > k, we want:
        #        R[k, j] = q_k^T * A[:, j]
        #        A[:, j] = A[:, j] - q_k * R[k, j]
        #
        #    We implement this in a row-wise, cache-friendly way that preserves
        #    the per-(k, j) accumulation order over i.

        # 3a. Initialize the part of row k of R above the diagonal.
        for j in [k + 1, N):
            R[k, j] = 0

        # 3b. Compute all inner products R[k, j] = Σ_i Q[i, k] * A[i, j] for j > k.
        #     We traverse row-wise: i outer, j inner.
        #     For a fixed k, different j > k are independent, so there are no cross-j
        #     dependencies during this accumulation.
        for i in [0, M):
            for j in [k + 1, N):
                R[k, j] += Q[i, k] * A[i, j]

        # 3c. Apply the rank-1 update A[:, j] -= Q[:, k] * R[k, j] for all j > k.
        #     Again traverse row-wise: i outer, j inner.
        for i in [0, M):
            for j in [k + 1, N):
                A[i, j] = A[i, j] - Q[i, k] * R[k, j]

optimization:
    # High-level intent:
    # - Keep the outer k loop sequential to respect the data dependence:
    #     the computation at step k+1 uses the updated A from step k.
    # - Reorder and tile i and j within each fixed k to:
    #     * align memory accesses with row-major layout (j innermost),
    #     * improve cache reuse by working on tiles of the trailing submatrix,
    #     * enable SIMD vectorization along contiguous memory (j),
    #     * exploit thread-level parallelism over independent columns j > k.

    # 1. Row/column blocking over the trailing submatrix (i, j>k).
    #
    #    At each k we conceptually operate on the trailing M × (N - (k+1)) submatrix of A and
    #    the corresponding row slice R[k, k+1:].
    #    We tile both the row dimension i and the column dimension j into I- and J-blocks.
    #
    #    This gives subproblems of size TI × TJ that fit better into L1/L2 cache
    #    and reduce capacity/conflict misses when M and N are large.
    block(i, I, TI)      # i  -> tiles of size TI: I is the block index for rows
    block(j, J, TJ)      # j  -> tiles of size TJ: J is the block index for columns (within j > k)

    # 2. Hoist the row/column tile loops directly under the k loop.
    #
    #    After blocking, re-order the loop nest for the trailing submatrix so that:
    #      k (sequential)
    #        J (column tiles)
    #          I (row tiles)
    #            i (rows within tile)
    #              j (columns within tile)
    #
    #    This maximizes reuse of:
    #      - the row slice of A and Q (fixed i, varying j) in the innermost loops,
    #      - the row k of R (fixed k, varying j) when accumulating and updating.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # 3. Access pattern and vectorization: j innermost, vectorized.
    #
    #    Because A and R are row-major, the j dimension is unit-stride for fixed i, k.
    #    We keep the j loops innermost inside each (I, J) tile and vectorize them, so that:
    #      - dot-product accumulation over j: R[k, j] += Q[i, k] * A[i, j]
    #      - rank-1 update:                A[i, j] -= Q[i, k] * R[k, j]
    #    both use contiguous loads/stores on A[i, j] and R[k, j].
    vectorize(j, VJ)     # SIMD across columns within a row; VJ matches hardware SIMD width
    unroll(j, VJ)        # Optionally unroll by the same factor to expose ILP to the compiler

    # 4. Scalar replacement for Q[i, k].
    #
    #    Within the inner loops at fixed (k, i), Q[i, k] is invariant across all j in a tile.
    #    We conceptually hoist each load of Q[i, k] into a scalar temporary (register)
    #    before the inner-most j loop, to avoid redundant memory accesses:
    #
    #      tmp_q = Q[i, k]
    #      for j in J-tile:
    #          R[k, j] += tmp_q * A[i, j]
    #      ...
    #      for j in J-tile:
    #          A[i, j] -= tmp_q * R[k, j]
    #
    #    This is a standard scalar-replacement / register promotion transformation.
    hoist_loads_of(Q[i, k])   # conceptual: promote Q[i, k] to a scalar in the i–inner loop body

    # 5. Parallelization over column tiles J for fixed k.
    #
    #    For each fixed k, different columns j > k are independent:
    #      - The dot products R[k, j] = Q[:, k]^T A[:, j] only read Q[:, k] and A[:, j].
    #      - The updates A[:, j] -= Q[:, k] * R[k, j] only touch A[:, j] and R[k, j].
    #    There is no write–write or write–read dependence across different j values
    #    within the same k, so we can parallelize across J tiles.
    #
    #    We keep the k loop outside the parallel region to preserve the inherently
    #    sequential dependence across k.
    parallelize(J)       # e.g., map J over OpenMP threads with an implicit barrier at each k

    # 6. Reduce divisions when forming Q.
    #
    #    Instead of performing M independent divisions Q[i, k] = A[i, k] / R[k, k],
    #    we can compute once per k:
    #
    #        inv_rkk = 1.0 / R[k, k]
    #        Q[i, k] = A[i, k] * inv_rkk
    #
    #    This replaces M divisions by 1 division + M multiplications, which is cheaper
    #    on most CPUs. Mathematically this is equivalent; rounding differences are negligible
    #    and typically smaller than those from the overall Gram–Schmidt process.
    precompute_reciprocal(R[k, k])   # conceptual: implement Q[:, k] using a single reciprocal per k

    # 7. Optional: tune remaining i-dimension structure.
    #

    #
```
